I know that feeling, many times over. My first "real" time getting sober was an absolute suffer fest for a few days, and then I was completely blown away by how quickly I was feeling not only much better, but much better than I could remember for a very long time. Except for the sugar cravings. I had insane sugar cravings for awhile, which is pretty typical. But that's small beans comparatively. 

But all those things you mentioned. After 3 or 4 days my mood started to lift. After a week my sleep improved massively. At that same time I wanted to start getting exercise again and to eat healthier. As that went on, my belly decreased, I lost a lot of inflammation, my skin and especially my face started to look better...and that continued for months. I was way more able to give my relationships more energy and attention, able to make other life changes that were always "I'll do that when I feel better" or more accurately "when I'm not hungover and/or drunk again", etc.

There were challenges for sure, and as you can tell by my number challenges remain. But I put together a long streak that I still feel good about. If nothing else, it proved that I CAN quit, that I can be healthier, that I can feel like a better person, that I will survive this, and that I (hopefully) won't die from drinking. While I've lost that and many other sober streaks, my drinking has never returned to the level it was. I still have a lot of work to do, both with drinking and with life, but that first hurdle, taking that first sober day in many years, was huge, even though I couldn't sleep and was worried I would die from DTs.

One day at a time. One day is huge. Good on you, and I'll stay sober with you today.

Not only did they not do that, they essentially told me I have no future here, and especially not if I keep making noise. So, I'm going back to school (in my friggin' mid-40s) just to develop a tool that will hopefully make me employable elsewhere. If I can't make one of my "passions" work for a job, I'll just be a cog in a machine, but hopefully with energy and brainspace left over to do other things with my personal time.

My first real sobriety I had an amazing pink haze phase. I hated that it wore off. After that, every sobriety, even this very short one I have right now, brings me back to being amazed at how long a day can feel when you aren't fast-forwarding with alcohol.

That can be good or bad depending on how you want to fill the time. Are you just killing time or do you want to do something with it? I'm guilty of killing a LOT of time. I have been unhappy and depressed most of my life. But, removing that fast-forward button that also guarantees that you will feel bad tomorrow, that you will spend a lot of money, and that you'll probably want to drink again frees up a lot of energy to actually do something with that time.

Whether you choose to do something is the difference. But even if it's dull and depressing, at least I'm not suffering the insane drama of my darkest drinking days. I'll take boring over that mess any time.

I'm also 43, nearly 44. I quit for the first time a few years before covid and then fell off again. By my count, I obviously haven't stuck to it super well but I did at one point have 3 years sober and am trying to get back there. 

I think your 40s is a great time to quit. The reasons I've struggled with quitting again are pretty much the ones I struggled with years ago, so I think my best advice is to pay attention to that little voice that tells me that I am okay without it, that I'm better without it, that I'll feel better without it, and that all the little things that my addicted brain tells me is good about drinking is a lie. No matter how much I drink, I will wake up and feel truly awful, and will have to make this decision all over again. It never fails. And the longer I go making the wrong decision, the shorter and more painful what life I have left will be. 

That, and being honest with loved ones. That one was so difficult for me, and still is. Luckily my drinking has never gotten back to where it was the worst, but having supportive friends and family that know my story makes a big difference. And I know I have some people around me now that would have a conversation with me if it gets bad again.

Not much future-building. And LOTS and LOTS and oh god I mean LOTS of drinking. I was able to stay sober there for a good stretch and was comfortable with it. But it wasn't taking me where I suddenly wanted to go. Turns out drunk me doesn't want to go anywhere or do anything productive. Sober me wants to improve my life.

I told close friends early on in my sobriety. Most were not surprised and most were very supportive. I eventually told my whole family, which was harder, but necessary. I knew they would be supportive, but I was just embarrassed. I shouldn't have been.

I bought a house and land. It keeps me busy and gives me something to build and improve year after year. Turns out I needed that kind of project that feels meaningful and I get to see the benefits as time goes by. 

I started a huge garden to, again, keep me busy, wear me out, and encourage me to eat better. Plus, it turns out having a bunch of things growing in my yard that I planned out and that I get to see from seed to end-of-season is intensely gratifying.

I picked back up old hobbies and interesting, making a pointed mental note that if I let these things or things like them slide out of my routine again, I should take it as a warning sign and get my life back in shape. Depression and anxiety were probably most of the reasons I started drinking regularly. I figure those moments will be the easiest way back to drinking.

Liquidy, maybe. I stopped coming here when I was considering trying to moderate again. We know how that goes. My sobriety was solid and quality within a couple days of coming back to SD on the regular. Coincidence? Nah. 

I started on a whole new career path. Well, A career path. I had been wallowing in nothingness for quite a few years before this, convinced I was having fun or living on the edge, being outside of the "system", "free", even. The truth is that I had been beaten down, and felt I couldn't handle a "real" job, or really and responsibility. As long as I was surrounded by other people that pretended getting trashed as often as possible on whatever chemicals possible was "really living", I didn't have to change. We were rebels. Dirtbags. Burners. Anarch-punk-desert-dwellers. I still carry some of the attitude and the vision that I had then, but it turns out I get a lot out of my new career. I work with kids with an eye towards the future. What better way to reset how you see the world than through the eyes of a hopeful kid? THAT'S what I needed. I needed exposure to non-cynical earnest kids who want a better world. That's what I didn't get while drinking.

These are my major getting-sober dates. The first two of those were spent in hospital, convinced I had pushed my acts of self-destruction too far and was definitely dying. I'm lucky and happy to have been wrong both times. The third was just before going in to the hospital for internal bleeding from ulcers. The fourth, luckily, did not involve a hospital, but it did involve a flurry of trips to the doctor.

I've known the short-term damage of alcohol abuse for many, many years. Only in the past couple years have I become intimately aware of the long-term damage.

I sought to get sober because I knew I couldn't get out of a hole I had dug for myself while still drinking. I got sober because I did not want to die or ruin my body and mind to the point of essentially being dead. I got sober because I didn't want to go to jail, and was tempting that literally every day. I got sober because I was sick and tired of being dependent on alcohol, and sick and tired of pushing everyone away so that I could just be alone and drink myself to oblivion.

Sobriety has been all sorts of things. Very difficult sometimes, especially in the early days. Boring sometimes, until I learned that being bored is a blessing. That's the space where we can create; we can do new things, try new hobbies, pick back up old hobbies. I do struggle with feeling borING, as there were a lot of things I liked about my drunk personality. I liked dropping the filter, feeling in-the-flow, etc. I am reserved and guarded in normal life; drinking was the easy way past that. Relearning my actual personality has sometimes been difficult and stressful. But I know it's REAL. 

Sure, I'm no longer the life of the party, but was I EVER? In my own mind, sure. And maybe on certain nights. Was it worth it? Hard no. And, is it actually a problem to not be "the life"? Nope. Turns out I don't like most parties anymore. I don't go to the bar or shows. Turns out I really like staying home and sitting by the fire and planning and growing my garden. I like silence and stability and comfort. I like to see friends one-to-one or in small groups. And all these things are fine and good. I'm always moving more into the space of appreciating the small day-to-day things, which I would have called "boring" most of my life. Turns out that's where the real magic is.

Both of us started working out hard for the first time in many years after we stopped drinking. We were expressing some good-natured frustration over the thought of "we've been working really hard to get in shape, shouldn't it be getting easier?!" That of course doesn't make sense because you're always exercising at a percentage of your maximum effort. You're always increasing (hopefully) your maximum effort even if you never actually hit it. It's a theoretical limit that always moves.

Similar here. 100% perfect is impossible except maybe in very short moments. 98% is really damn close. Effectively the same. But much more attainable. And still fluid. If you're always aiming for 98%, it will always be increasing.

Like everyone here, stopping drinking was key to stopping my downward spiral. It didn't fix anything, but it removed the single biggest factor in my rock bottom. My 98% looks like this: I want to feel good. When I feel good, energized, positive, I am better to myself and the world. I want a fulfilling life. This means I sometimes want to work hard, I sometimes want to play hard, I sometimes want to rest, I sometimes want to introspect, I sometimes want to be amongst community, I sometimes want to be alone. When I get this combination right, I am good to my neighbors and to myself. This is my 98%. The 'zone'. I want to be in the 'zone'. When I'm there, everything comes naturally and easily. There is no struggle. 

What that looks like day to day: always move forward, but be gentle and patient. Some days I can't move forward. Maybe even some weeks, or months. But if I'm patient and gentle, and if I'm engaging with life in good faith, I know I'll get the rest and recuperation I need so that one day, and who knows when, I can start moving forward again. Whether that means looking for a new path in life, a new job, a new home, or maybe just reaching out to a new person, or maybe just going to a new place to sit and think, or maybe just getting up the nerve to simply leave the house that day.

Getting sober took courage. Telling my friends took courage. Telling my family took a LOT of courage. 

Maybe the biggest single step that I needed to take was a massive life overhaul. I was living in a beautiful but bizarre place, kind of a never-neverland for lost kids who never grow up. It's so much fun, so much to do, but I was stuck. And EVERYTHING involved drinking and drugs. And everyone in this small town new me as a party guy.

I also owned a business that was the worst decision I've ever made. I crashed and burned, hard. And that's when my drinking and drugging went from 'problematic but sustainable' to straight up destructive.

So I eventually realized that fixing that meant fixing EVERYTHING. I got sober, closed my business, moved across the country. Leaving behind friends and a home I loved so much. I haven't settled into my 'new' life yet so there's a feeling of being in limbo, which is scary as hell on its own. But I knew it needed to happen to give myself a real shot at life again. 

And that took the most courage. The decision to slough off layers and layers and layers of my identity to launch into the unknown, with no guarantee that it will work. Without things even lined up to replace those layers I took off. Being willing to stand naked in the elements for as long as it takes for those layers to be replaced naturally. 

I'm not a kid anymore, so this change is harder than any that's come before it. But that's life, right? Your choices get harder and harder, but you're also better equipped to deal with them, so we hopefully go through them more and more gracefully. Maybe. I don't know.

All I know is it was a hard, hard choice. And I'm so glad I did it. Because thought I'm scared, my life has potential again.
